issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s regular payment of rent at intervals longer than a month, willingly accepted without complaint by the landlord, may establish a contrary agreement and prevent those payments from amounting to habitual default.
material_facts: The tenant had been paying rent every three or four months over a period of time.
The landlord willingly accepted those payments without complaint about their timing.
The tenant was not in arrears when the eviction proceedings began.
The Rent Controller and the Collector found that the tenant was not a habitual defaulter.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was not a habitual defaulter, and the High Court ought not to have interfered with that finding.
issues.legal_principle: A monthly tenant is ordinarily obliged to pay rent monthly, but the parties may make a contrary agreement. Such an agreement need not be in writing and may be inferred from their conduct over a fairly long period. The judgment cites no particular statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The dispute is an eviction proceeding concerning a tenant’s alleged default in paying rent.
predicates.tenant_regularly_pays_rent_at_longer_int: The tenant repeatedly pays rent at intervals longer than the ordinary monthly interval.
predicates.landlord_accepts_delayed_rent_without_co: The landlord accepts those delayed payments without objecting to their timing.
predicates.tenant_not_in_arrears_when_proceedings_b: The tenant owes no rent when the eviction proceeding begins.

issues.definition: When a tenant in an eviction proceeding repeatedly pays rent late, the landlord accepts those payments without complaint, and no rent is outstanding when proceedings begin, the tenant is not a habitual defaulter.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising supervisory jurisdiction should not disturb concurrent factual findings of rent tribunals where the evidence supports those findings and the High Court’s intervention would cause injustice.
material_facts: The Rent Controller and the Collector both found that the tenant was not a habitual defaulter.
The evidence accepted by those tribunals showed that the landlord had willingly accepted rent paid every three or four months without complaint.
The High Court accepted the landlord’s contention and interfered with the concurrent finding.
The Supreme Court considered that intervention an excess of the High Court’s narrow jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the limits of its narrow supervisory jurisdiction and ought not to have interfered with the concurrent finding; its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 confers narrow supervisory jurisdiction, which did not permit the High Court to interfere with the concurrent factual findings in these circumstances. The judgment refers generally to several earlier decisions of the Supreme Court but names none.

rule.if: high_court_supervisory_review and concurrent_factual_findings and evidence_supports_concurrent_findings and high_court_disturbs_findings

predicates.high_court_supervisory_review: The High Court is reviewing a lower tribunal’s decision in the exercise of supervisory jurisdiction.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: Two lower tribunals have made the same factual finding.
predicates.evidence_supports_concurrent_findings: Evidence accepted by the lower tribunals supports their shared factual finding.
predicates.high_court_disturbs_findings: The High Court sets aside or alters the shared factual finding.

issues.definition: When the High Court exercises supervisory review and disturbs concurrent factual findings supported by evidence, that intervention is improper.
